content.body: Have you ever looked at a map and wondered how many separate islands or landmasses exist? In coding, we face similar problems with connected components. Today, we'll learn how to count them efficiently using a clever memory technique.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain what connected components are in a graph
2. Implement a visited tracking system using a hash map
3. Count components by traversing unvisited nodes
4. Apply this pattern to solve similar connectivity problems
5. Recognize when to check vs. add to your memory structure
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Look at this simple graph with 3 nodes: 0-1 are connected, 2 is alone. How many connected components do you see?
content.successMessage: Exactly! There are 2 components: one with nodes 0 and 1, and another with just node 2.

content.title: Try a bigger graph
content.prompt: Now try this graph with 5 nodes: 0-1-2 are connected, 3-4 are connected. How many components?
content.successMessage: Perfect! You identified 2 components: the chain 0-1-2 and the pair 3-4.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: Last one: 6 nodes where 0-1, 2-3-4, and 5 are all separate. How many components?
content.successMessage: Great! You manually traced through and found 3 separate groups. That's exactly what we need to automate.

content.body: What you just did was manual exploration: you looked at each node, followed its connections, and mentally grouped them. For small graphs, this works, but it's tedious and error-prone for larger ones.
content.title: What you did

content.body: Imagine a social network with millions of users. Manually tracing connections would be impossible! We need a systematic way to track which users we've already visited to avoid infinite loops and double-counting. Can't figure out how? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to remember what we have already seen. We'll use a lookup structure (like a Set or object) as our 'notebook' where we write down visited nodes. Before exploring a node, we check our notebook: if it's already there, we skip it; if not, we add it and explore all its connections. This prevents re-scanning and ensures we count each component exactly once.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like exploring a maze with a notebook. Each time you enter a new room, you write its name in your notebook. Before entering any room, you check your notebook - if it's already there, you don't go in again. This way you systematically map out all connected rooms without retracing your steps.

content.body: We'll use depth-first search (DFS) with a visited Set. For each unvisited node, we start a new component count and explore all connected nodes, marking them as visited in our Set.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Create a visited Set to track explored nodes
2. Initialize component count to 0
3. For each node in the graph:
   - If node is not in visited Set:
     - Increment component count
     - Start DFS/BFS from this node
     - Mark all reachable nodes as visited
4. Return the component count

content.body:
Congratulations! You've learned how to count connected components using a visited Set to remember what we've already seen. Key takeaways:
1. Always track visited nodes to avoid infinite loops
2. Each new DFS call on an unvisited node represents a new component
3. The 'check before add' pattern (if (!visited.has(node))) is crucial
4. This pattern applies to many graph problems - whenever you need to explore connections without repetition.

Remember: Your visited Set is like a notebook - check it before entering new territory, and update it as you explore!
